Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:7: And in the Tikkunim (25b) it appears that one must intend the aforementioned Name even while engaged in performing a mitzvah. There Rashbi, peace be upon him, explains the matter of YHVH, that it is Yod-Heh, awe and love, Vav-Heh, Torah and mitzvah; and he says: Vav is Torah, resting in the mouth and in the breath of the mouth, for Chochmah and Binah are hidden in the brain and heart, in love and awe, and Torah without awe and love does not fly upward, and so on. Heh Ze'irah (the lesser Heh) is the form of Adam, through which YHVH is completed, and she is the Heh, the holy Kingdom (Malchut); she is the mitzvah, the performance of the commandments, resting within the two hundred forty-eight limbs; and concerning Torah and mitzvah it is said, "the revealed things are for us" — Vav-Heh, revealed for us and for our children forever; and a mitzvah without awe and love cannot ascend before YHVH, who is the sum total of all — above all is Adam, Yod-Kei-Vav-Kei, the thought that rises to Ein Sof (the Infinite) — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:8: The intent of Rashbi, peace be upon him, is to explain that the Name YHVH should always be complete, whether one is occupied with Torah or with a mitzvah; therefore, in the occupation with Torah, it is Vav resting in the mouth and the breath of the mouth — meaning the mouth is Heh, the breath of the mouth is Vav. The explanation of this is that the mouth is Heh, since in the mouth are the five points of articulation by which speech is cut; Vav, the breath of the mouth, is the voice that goes out from the windpipe, in which are the rings, as is explained in Ra'aya Meheimna (Parashat Pinchas 235a-b); therefore it explains in the Tikkunim (145b) that voice and speech are Vav-Heh. And with awe and love, which are Yod-Heh — behold, YHVH.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:9: And so regarding mitzvah, Rashbi, peace be upon him, was precise in his wording, saying, "Heh Ze'irah is the form of Adam, through which YHVH is completed" — what is meant by "the form of Adam" here? And he then says, "she is the mitzvah, the performance of the commandments," and so on. Rather, the matter is as Rashbi explains elsewhere (131b), that a mitzvah is the completion of YHVH, because MiTZVaH by the At-Bash cipher is Yod-Heh, and YHVH transposed by At-Bash is Mem-Tzadi-Peh-Tzadi, and so on, as explained there — thus, in the word "mitzvah," YHVH [is contained]. And this is because the Shechinah has the whole of Atzilut portrayed within her, for she is comprised of the ten, and this is why she is called "the form of Adam." Therefore it says "she is the mitzvah." And to be precise about how YHVH is found within her, it elaborates further, saying "she is the mitzvah, the performance of the commandments, resting within the two hundred forty-eight limbs" — meaning that the reality of deed comes from her, who is Heh, and she rests within the two hundred forty-eight limbs, which is Vav — for the two hundred forty-eight limbs of a person are from the side of the male, and correspondingly there are two hundred forty-eight positive commandments from the right, corresponding to the two hundred forty-eight limbs, since the male leans to the right; and the three hundred sixty-five sinews correspond to the negative commandments, from the left, since the female leans to the left. And "a mitzvah without awe and love cannot ascend..." — behold, YHVH — for awe and love are Yod-Heh.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:10: And the Name Yod-Heh comes by the transposition of At-Bash within the word MiTZVaH — the reason being that Vav-Heh are revealed, as the verse says, "the revealed things," whereas love and awe are hidden in the brain and heart, and therefore they come as hidden, in a transposition of letters; and therefore, if a mitzvah lacks love and awe, the mitzvah is not completed so that YHVH rests upon it and it ascends above. It follows that both in Torah and in mitzvah, YHVH must be completed through awe and love, as explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:11: Afterward one must intend the mystery of thought, which is Yod-Kei-Vav-Kei (spelled out), to raise everything up to Ein Sof; and through this Name the Infinite [light] rests and spreads its light within the attributes. For this reason Rashbi, peace be upon him, called it in the Tikkunim (17a) "the watering of the tree from within," and therefore one must intend this Name in order to draw the light of Ein Sof, blessed be He, into His attributes. See in the Tikkunim how greatly Rashbi, peace be upon him, elaborated on the greatness of this Name.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:12: This is the essence of everything: first to rectify the supernal attributes, which are His thrones, blessed be He, in order to cause the light of the Emanator, Ein Sof, blessed and exalted be He, to rest upon them; and the essential intention of a person's thought in his prayer and Torah study is always to intend the essence of everything, that which sustains everything — Ein Sof, blessed and exalted be He. And so Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained (Zohar Parashat Vayakhel 213b): through these mysteries a person can attach himself to his Master — with the will directed by the intention of his heart to know the dominion of Chochmah in the supernal mystery. When he serves his Master in prayer, let his will cling like a flame to a coal, to unify those lower firmaments on the side of holiness, to crown them with one lower Name; and from there onward, to unify those supernal inner firmaments, so that all become one within that supernal firmament that stands over them. And while his mouth and lips move, let his heart direct its will to ascend higher and higher, to unify everything in the mystery of mysteries, where all wills and thoughts are anchored, in the mystery that stands within Ein Sof. This applies in every single prayer, to direct body and soul to this, every single day, to crown one's days with the mystery of the supernal days in his service — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:13: Now, having explained the essence of the holiness of thought, we need to explain what preparations are needed for the holiness of thought, so that thought may always cleave to Him, blessed be He, and to His Torah, whether one is occupied with his labor, or walking, or lying down, or rising — and his love for Him, blessed be He, should never depart from him, just as His love, blessed be He, always cleaves to us.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:14: We shall say that just as the mystery of the supernal Thought rests upon the attributes only through the rectification of the attributes that are below it, which serve as its throne — as is known, that when there is a blemish in the attributes, Imma withdraws from the Structure (Binyan), and all the more so Chochmah, and when the Mother returns to the children, which is called "teshuvah" (repentance/return), Chochmah too returns — so too in the reality of the holiness of thought: a person cannot sanctify his thought to be attached to his God unless he first sanctifies all his limbs, purifying them first through proper repentance, and afterward sanctifying them, as we shall explain below, please God, in detail, several kinds of holinesses. These are, in general, the holiness of sight, hearing, smell, and speech, which are explained in the Tikkunim and Ra'aya Meheimna to correspond to the Name YHVH. And afterward he should sanctify four others corresponding to the Name Adonai, which are: touch, motion, [sexual] pleasure, walking — as is explained in the Tikkunim (Tikkunei Zohar Chadash 99a), that this means touch with the hands, motion of the body, pleasure through the Covenant, walking with the feet; and it writes, in these words: and some say pleasure with the hands, touch (usage) with the Covenant, and all is true — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:15: Once all the vessels of the body are pure and holy, thought will rest within them; but if there is any blemish in the limbs, there is a defect there, for "whoever has a blemish shall not come near" (Leviticus 21:18), and the neshamah withdraws entirely, and that kelipah rests there and disturbs a person's thought in his prayer and Torah study, and it is impossible for him to have any attachment whatsoever. This is especially so if his tongue is blemished by evil speech and the like, since the tongue is a ladder for the ascent of Torah and prayer, and therefore an evil thought disturbs him so that he not effect a unification through it. Similarly with the other blemishes — being blemished, it is impossible for him to unify [the sefirot] in his prayer, for prayer is the bringing near and unification of the attributes through the Cause of Causes, and the Cause of Causes rests only upon a rectified throne.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:16: In particular, regarding what we explained in the Gate of Love (ch. 2), that a person's essential attachment to his Maker is the attachment of his soul to the root of life, as explained regarding the love bound up in "kisses" — see there — when the neshamah is blemished, there is an outsider there, and it cannot cleave to the supernal light. But once the neshamah is properly rectified, it becomes a throne for the supernal spirituality, and can attach itself to the Soul of All, wherein lies the essential attachment. On the necessity of this we quoted several passages from Rashbi, peace be upon him, in the Gate of Awe, chapters 9 and 10 — see there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:17: The general way for a person to sanctify and purify his limbs is through purity (taharah) and holiness (kedushah), as explained in Ra'aya Meheimna (Parashat Pinchas 245b), whose wording we quoted above in chapter 4 — namely, purity on the inside and holiness on the outside; and there Rashbi, peace be upon him, explains that these two are acquired through occupation with Torah. However, as we wrote in the Gate of Love, chapter 8, regarding purity, that the essential purification is through fire, and one who sits in fasting purifies himself through the boiling of his fat and blood, melted by the fire that weakens his body. Yet our Rabbis, of blessed memory, also explained (Ta'anit 11a-b) that one who sits in fasting is called "holy" — showing that its essential aspect is holiness, and this holiness is the right side, as it is written, "the merciful man does good to his own soul" (Proverbs 11:17) — see what I wrote there — while purity, it is said, is essentially through immersion in a mikveh, as we elaborated above in chapter 8; and this fits somewhat with "purity on the inside," since through this the neshamah is purified from within. Both of these are necessarily required of a penitent, for since he is blemished, mere occupation with Torah will not help to purify and sanctify him — for to the wicked, God says, "What have you to do with declaring My statutes?" (Psalms 50:16) — therefore he must first purify himself through immersion, and afterward sanctify himself through fasting, afflicting himself in place of what he indulged in, as we shall elaborate in the Gate of Repentance, please God; and afterward the purity and holiness will benefit through words of Torah, and the Torah will complete for him the purity and holiness — for if he does not occupy himself with Torah, what will all his repentance avail him? Thus he would have no purity and holiness in the full completeness required. These are the two general aspects for acquiring holiness.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:18: Further required for acquiring holiness is the holiness of place, as we find mentioned in the Torah, in Parashat Acharei Mot (Leviticus 16:24), "a holy place." There are two aspects to this: either the place is made holy through occupation with Torah and prayer, such as a study hall or synagogue; or it is holy [in the sense of being] a place separated and set apart from people — a place secluded from people is a great preparation for attachment [to God], and therefore the early sages would separate themselves from settled society and were called the "circle of the secluded ones," as the pious author of Chovot HaLevavot brings (Gate of Trust, ch. 4; see Gate of Separation, ch. 3); and it is one of the conditions of separation (perishut) to desire solitude, for by this a person demonstrates in his soul that he has no bond at all with the people of this world — as is true after his passing — and therefore, from now on, he demonstrates his soul's status as a stranger in this world, and does not wish to attach himself to anyone except his God, blessed be He, to whom he is destined to be truly attached, if he merits it.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:19: And so it is written in Chovot HaLevavot (Gate of Trust, ibid.) regarding a certain ascetic who entered a certain country to instruct its inhabitants in divine service, and found them wearing one color in their garments, and saw their graves near the entrances of their houses, and saw no woman among them, and he asked them, and they answered him regarding each matter as explained there in Chovot HaLevavot. And to the third question, that he saw no woman among them, they answered him: what you have seen, that we have separated from women and children — know that we have set aside for them a nearby town; one of us, when he needs something of theirs, goes to them and completes his need and returns to us — because we have seen what would come upon us of distraction of the heart, great loss, and great toil and trouble from closeness to them, and the rest from all this comes from distancing ourselves, to choose the matters of the World to Come and to despise this world.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:20: And so with the prophet Elisha we find that he had a holy place prepared for his holiness — what the Shunammite woman did for him, as it is written, "Behold now, I perceive that this is a holy man of God, who passes by us continually; let us make, I pray you, a small upper chamber on the wall, and let us set for him there a bed, a table, a chair, and a lamp" (II Kings 4:9-10). This shows that because of his holiness, he needed a prepared place, namely a small upper chamber, which is a place somewhat separated from people, and the necessary natural provisions used by ordinary people — namely a bed, table, chair, and lamp — which is a moderate degree of separation, as the pious author of Chovot HaLevavot wrote (Gate of Separation, ch. 3), regarding the three classes among ascetics, and among those who seclude themselves in their own homes is the second class, which is closer to the way of Torah — see there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:21: These are the two aspects of the holiness of place. And if it is possible for both to be combined — such as a person's seclusion in his study hall or synagogue — how good is his portion, for he will certainly acquire an added holiness for his soul. And so our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Yalkut Tehillim, remez 872): the Holy One, blessed be He, said, whoever occupies himself with Torah and acts of kindness and is found (matzui) in the synagogue, it is as though he redeemed Me and My children from among the nations of the world — so far his words. And the word "found" (matzui) indicates constancy in the synagogue, for just as other people, when sought, are known to be found in the places where they usually sit most of the day, and are sought there, so this man is found most of the day's time in the synagogue, until, when one person asks another, "Where is so-and-so to be found?" they answer him that he is to be found in the synagogue. Let him learn from what was commanded of the High Priest, "and he shall not go out from the sanctuary" (Leviticus 21:12) — in this manner, one who wishes to sanctify himself should sanctify himself in the holy place, the synagogue or the study hall.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:22: Nevertheless, seclusion is best acquired together with a companion, for they said, of blessed memory (Berachot 63b), "A sword is upon the boasters (badim), and they shall become fools" (Jeremiah 50:36), and so on, as will be explained, please God. And they said, of blessed memory, in the Sifrei (Yalkut Bamidbar, remez 976), on the verse, "Two are better than one" (Ecclesiastes 4:9): from here they said, a person should acquire a companion for himself, to read with him, to study with him, to eat with him, and to reveal his secrets to him — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:23: The proper manner of separation and holiness for Torah scholars who separate from their wives from Sabbath to Sabbath is that they should choose for themselves a special house, separate from the house in which they live with their wives, and prepare for their own sustenance and that of their households one day a week; and by this they will conduct themselves in holiness of speech and the other holinesses that will be explained — for as long as a person is busy going in and out to the marketplace, he cannot avoid evil speech or anger, or at least he will sin by improper sight; whereas separation in a special house saves a person from all this. This is the straight path that one who wishes to sanctify himself should choose for himself.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:24: Further among the things that add holiness and are beneficial for the holiness of thought is when a person fulfills the commandments of tzitzit and tefillin, in their performance and in their proper intention. Regarding the commandment of tzitzit, holiness is explicitly mentioned in the Torah: "That you may remember and do all My commandments, and be holy unto your God" (Numbers 15:40). And they said, of blessed memory, in the Sifrei, in these words: "That you may remember and do" — to make a remembrance like the deed. "And be holy" — this is the holiness of all the commandments. Or is it only the holiness of tzitzit? Regarding what is the matter speaking, the holiness of all the commandments? Rabbi says, this is the holiness of tzitzit. Or is it perhaps the holiness of all the commandments? When it says, "You shall be holy" (Leviticus 19:2), behold, the holiness of all the commandments has already been stated. So what does the verse teach by "and be holy"? This is the holiness of tzitzit — teaching that tzitzit adds holiness to Israel — so far their words. This makes explicit, according to Rabbi, that tzitzit adds holiness.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:25: It is possible to say the reason, as explained above in chapter 4, from the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him, that all holiness is from the outside, as is written (Parashat Chayei Sarah, beginning of 125b), "the assistance of his Master surrounds him, and he is called holy" — and the reason is explained there. Now, the commandment of tzitzit is a commandment in which a person wraps himself, and the mitzvah, in its holiness, surrounds him on all sides — therefore it adds holiness.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:26: And so the commandment of tefillin, our Rabbis, of blessed memory, called "holiness," in saying (Megillah 26b) regarding the straps, that they are utensils of holiness (tashmishei kedushah), while the tallit is a utensil of mitzvah (tashmish mitzvah); and so the wording of Rashbi, peace be upon him, regarding tzitzit and tefillin, is repeatedly "the separation of mitzvah and holiness" — that tefillin are a higher holiness than tzitzit, for tzitzit is called mitzvah while tefillin is called holiness.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:27: The commentators, of blessed memory, agree (Rabbeinu Yonah, Berachot 8a in the Rif's pages) that placing the tefillin on the arm opposite the heart and upon the head is in order to subjugate to the Holy One, blessed be He, one's brain and heart, which are the primary limbs of a person, upon which life depends and upon which thoughts depend, as explained at the beginning of this chapter; and the intent is that through the holiness of the twenty-one mentions [of the Divine Name] written in the hand-tefillin and the twenty-one in the head-tefillin, corresponding to Ehyeh Asher Ehyeh, as is explained in the Tikkunim (27b). There is no doubt that when the mentions [of the Name] within the tefillin are written with the proper intention, as Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained in Parashat Vayikra (11b) and Parashat Acharei Mot (65b), and likewise the rectification of the boxes (batim), their squareness and stitching properly done, and the straps and knots properly made — [these serve] to purify one's thoughts and cause one's thought to cleave to YHVH, for the tefillin are placed in the location of thought.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:28: Now, since these two commandments pertain to the subject we are engaged in, we shall discuss what is found in the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him, pertaining to the intent of the mitzvah — for one who performs the mitzvah with its proper intention is not comparable to one who performs it without intention, since through the intention one gives the mitzvah an ascent, that it may rise above, as Rashbi, peace be upon him, explains (Tikkunei Zohar 25b), which we quoted, saying, "a mitzvah without awe and love cannot ascend before..."; and through knowing the intent of the mitzvah, he places in his heart awe and love, by knowing what rectification he performs through that mitzvah — but if he does not know its intent, the tefillin remain on his brain and arm like mere stones, and do not arouse in his heart any awe or love.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:29: Regarding the tallit itself, it is proper, ideally, to endeavor that it be made of wool, and the Nimmukei Yosef, peace be upon him, elaborated in the minor halachot of the Rif, of blessed memory, that the Geonim and most of the commentators agreed on this; and he writes at the end of his words, of blessed memory: therefore one should make only a tallit fringed with wool, so as to fulfill the biblical commandment of tzitzit with it; and I have already so taught publicly, and this is the accepted practice — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:30: According to the plain meaning, the intent of wrapping in tzitzit is to teach a person to remember all the commandments through seeing the tekhelet (blue thread), as it says, "and you shall see it and remember all the commandments of the Lord" (Numbers 15:39). And how does the tekhelet indicate remembrance of them? This can be understood from what our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Chullin 89a): it was taught, Rabbi Meir used to say, why is tekhelet different from all other colors? Because tekhelet resembles the sea, and the sea resembles the sky, and the sky resembles the Throne of Glory, as it is said, "and under His feet was, as it were, a paved work of sapphire stone..." (Exodus 24:10), and it is written, "as the appearance of a sapphire stone was the likeness of a throne" (Ezekiel 1:26) — so far his words. And although this passage has a mystical dimension, as is explained at the end of Parashat Shelach Lecha (Zohar 175b), nevertheless, according to the plain meaning, it alludes to the quarrying-place of the souls, which are from the Throne of Glory, as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said, that the souls of the righteous are hewn from beneath the Throne of Glory. And when a person remembers the root of his soul, that it is from the Throne, and there his soul shall return, as it is written, "and the spirit shall return to God who gave it" (Ecclesiastes 12:7) — and "the Throne" (HaKisei) numerically equals "Elohim" — he will come to fulfill the commandments, and will sanctify himself with the holiness of the supernal ones, and will separate from the desires of the world. This is [the meaning of] "and you shall not go astray after your heart and after your eyes, after which you go astray, that you may remember..." (Numbers 15:39) "and be holy unto your God." The intent of "unto your God" is that with Him you shall be attached, ultimately, after the perishing of materiality; and God rests upon the Throne, and there are the Seraphim who say "Holy."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:31: It may be for this reason that the dye of the chilazon (the snail from which tekhelet was made) was such that the chilazon appeared only once every seventy years, as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained (Menachot 44a), to allude to the days of our years, which are seventy years (Psalms 90:10). Therefore it is explained that all colors are auspicious to see in a dream except for the color tekhelet, which indicates absolute judgment, being the ultimate end of all things, the judgment of souls, as is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Terumah, end of 152a), in these words: all colors are good to see in a dream except tekhelet, as has been stated, because it is the throne for judging the judgments of souls, and so on — see there. And this is the reason for "and you shall see it and remember," and so on, as is explained there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:32: It seems to me that this mystery is alluded to in the portion of tzitzit, in the words, "and it shall be to you for a fringe (tzitzit)" (Numbers 15:39) — the final letters spelling "HaMet" (the dead) — for the matter of remembering [via] the tzitzit is to remember the day of death, through the chilazon, as explained. And further, "and you shall see it and you shall remember" — the final letters equal, in numerical value, "Elohim," which equals "HaKisei" (the Throne) — that is, the Throne by which judgments of souls are judged.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:33: And in the Zohar, at the end of Parashat Shelach Lecha (175b), it explains that the entire commandment of tzitzit is a testimony to testify to a person concerning the service of his Maker. It says there: how many witnesses did the Creator make to testify concerning a person! And it says regarding tzitzit: he wraps himself in the wrapping of the mitzvah, in the four corners of his garment; four kings emerge to meet the four; four true witnesses of the King hang from the four corners.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:34: This passage is from the Sifra DeTzniuta, the fifth chapter, and its wording, at the end of Parashat Terumah (179a), is: four kings emerge to meet the four, on which hang [the tassels] like grapes in a cluster, in which are bound seven runners, testifying testimony, yet not standing in their place — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:35: All this statement is explained there, at the end of Parashat Shelach Lecha, where it says that the "seven runners" mentioned are the seven windings of the tekhelet thread, that must be wound in each and every one, either three times or up to thirteen; whoever adds should not add beyond them, and whoever reduces should not reduce below seven. And it further says there, Rabbi Yitzchak said, seven windings, for she is the Shechinah, the seventh of all, certainly, since she is blessed from the six others through the [agency of the] Righteous One; and if there are thirteen [windings], it is as they established, corresponding to the thirteen measures [of mercy], and this is the opening of them all.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:36: And it further says: we have learned that Yesod and the root are crowned together in the King, and this is the remembrance and the opening to all the other crowns, as it is written, "Open to me the gates of righteousness" (Psalms 118:19), and it is written, "this is the gate of the Lord..." and it is written, "and you shall see it and remember all the commandments of the Lord" (Numbers 15:39), to include in this all the other crowns; and therefore they are witnesses testifying testimony yet not standing in their place, because it is a mitzvah, and we have learned, utensils of a mitzvah may be discarded [after use].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:37: Further on, Rabbi Yitzchak said, these threads show how they hang from here and from there to the four directions of the world from this place, and she [the Shechinah] rules over all in the mystery of the heart, for she is the heart of the whole world, and the heart of those above, and depends on the supernal heart, and everything is in the heart that emerges from the supernal Chochmah.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:38: Further on Rabbi Yehudah said, the Holy One, blessed be He, said: whoever wishes to walk after My fear (yirah) shall walk after this heart, and after the eyes that stand upon her — who are these eyes? As it is said, "The eyes of the Lord are toward the righteous" (Psalms 34:16). "But you shall not go astray after your heart and after your eyes" — why? "After which you go astray" — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:39: It follows from the sum of the words of this passage that the four tzitzit are four witnesses, and likewise the seven windings are seven witnesses, as it says in the Sifra DeTzniuta, "seven runners testifying testimony." The mystery of these witnesses is well explained in the words of Rabbi Yehudah, who said, "who are these eyes? As it is said, 'The eyes of the Lord are toward the righteous.'" These are the "eyes" of Ze'ir [Anpin] explained in the Zohar (Parashat Naso 136b), where it says there: from those colors that are revealed emerge seven watching eyes that come from the black of the eye — this is what is written, "upon one stone, seven eyes" (Zechariah 3:9); which "one stone"? The black of the eye. From the red emerge seven runners that support the left side, blazing in fire toward the north, and unite to spread out in the world, to reveal the ways of the wicked; this is what is written, "these seven are the eyes of the Lord, they range through all the earth" (Zechariah 4:10). From the green emerge seven pure ones bound to the south side, and unite to spread out in the world to reveal deeds, as it is written, "for His eyes are upon the ways of man..." (Job 34:21) — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:40: It follows that when a person contemplates this hint of the witnesses standing and testifying concerning him at every time and every moment, he will fear to sin, and will be careful in the performance of the commandments; and this is the hint of the commandment of tzitzit, in brief — let the intelligent reader delve into these words and know them.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:41: Regarding the windings of the tzitzit, it is fitting that they number thirty-nine (tal), as is explained in Ra'aya Meheimna (Parashat Pinchas 228b), in these words, on the reason for the mitzvah and its matter, in brief: one-third [of the fringe should be] a knotted braid, and two-thirds a loose fringe, which is Tiferet. And every section (chuliah) is threefold — for everything threefold is from the side of holiness, as it is written (in the order of the Kedushah) "Holy unto You, they shall say thrice-holy," and Israel is a third [nation] because it is "a third over all" (Exodus 14:7, homiletically) — for the tzitzit is from the side of the middle pillar, which is the third of the Patriarchs. And every threefold matter — Heh-Vav, Yod-Lamed-Yod — every word is threefold from its side; a section comprised of three threefold windings is the Shechinah, "Holy unto You they shall say thrice-holy," and she is threefold in the middle pillar, comprising the three branches of the Patriarchs, which are the Shin of "Shabbat," and the Shechinah is the only daughter, filled with the tekhelet that is in the tzitzit. Fortunate is the body that is thus marked with the Shechinah, and the Holy One, blessed be He, is upon the wings of the mitzvah, marked in the strap that is the hand-tefillah with three windings around the middle finger, which is like the section wound in three windings around a finger. It is marked in the knot of the tefillin, comprised of two knots; fifteen threefold [windings] ascend, two in one knot. There are thirteen sections, containing thirty-nine windings, numerically equal to "tal" (39), and the thirteen sections equal, numerically, one (echad); together they equal 52 (Ben), and this is "Ben Yah," the middle pillar — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:42: And there (228a) they say that the mystery of "tal" (39) is Yod-Kei-Vav, which numerically equals 39, and the final Heh is the Shechinah, which completes Yod-Kei-Vav-Kei — that is, Adam (numerically 45). It appears the intent is a hint to the five knots. And it further says, the knot of the tallit is "the living one of the worlds" (chai olamim), for the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah are bound on all sides to the four corners of the tallit — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:43: And there (227a) it says that the mystery of the tallit is in the mystery of Metatron, and Metatron is composed of four living creatures and six ascents to the Throne, and in the Throne there are seventy-two bridges, and correspondingly there is in the tzitzit a hint to seventy-two, between the knots and sections, which are thirteen sections and five knots on each side, equaling eighteen (chai), and four times eighteen equal seventy-two; and this is likewise explained in the Tikkunim (Tikkun 10, 25b), and this is [the meaning of] "and a throne shall be established in kindness (chesed)" (Isaiah 16:5), for Chesed numerically equals seventy-two.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:44: And it says (Ra'aya Meheimna 227a) that the hint of the threads is thirty-two, corresponding to Yod-Heh-Heh-Vav (spelled out), and the Vav is a hint to the thirteen sections, to complete Adam — Yod-Kei-Vav-Kei — within Metatron, whose name is like the name of his Master. In these words: every living creature has four faces and four wings — these are thirty-two faces and wings, and they depend on the living creature (chayah) which is Adam, and they are thirty-two, numerically equal to Yod-Heh-Heh; the completion is Vav, thirteen sections in each of the four corners. The eight threads for each corner correspond to the four faces and four wings of each living creature, which are the four faces [corresponding to] YHVH and the four wings [corresponding to] Adonai — so far his words; and afterward it says, thus is found YAHDONHY (the combined Name) on every side.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:45: In this very same wording it says in the Tikkunim (25b): whoever wraps himself in the wrapping of the mitzvah is as though he had established a throne for the Holy One, blessed be He; and these [letters] YAHDONHY, each ascending to four faces and four wings, total 64 (Samekh-Dalet), and the eight letters of YAHDONHY total 72 (Ayin-Bet) — so far his words. And it further says afterward (26a) that the hint of the eight threads corresponds to the four faces and four wings, the numerical value of Shaddai by the small reckoning (mispar katan).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:46: Further, regarding the hint of the mitzvah, it is quoted at the end of Parashat Shelach Lecha (175a) from the commandments of Rashbi, peace be upon him (see Parashat Pinchas 257a); it says there that the mystery of the tekhelet in the tzitzit is the harsh Judgment that consumes and destroys everything, and therefore, because of the Judgment, it is said, "and you shall see it and remember all My commandments" (Numbers 15:40) — like a son who sees the strap and fears to sin against his father, out of fear of the strap.
